Because the residual stream is a sum of component outputs, each attention head or MLP's direct push toward a token is its output dotted with that token's unembedding row W_U[t]. Variant: the tuned lens adds a learned linear map per layer.
used_for: nostalgebraist's logit lens (2020), the tuned lens (Belrose and colleagues, 2023), the TransformerLens library and circuit studies such as indirect-object identification (2022). In the book: Only here.

name: Activation patching and attribution patching
formula: Patching effect = M(run on prompt A with activation a_c replaced by its value from prompt B) − M(clean run on A); normalized: (M_patched − M_corrupt) ÷ (M_clean − M_corrupt); attribution patching: ΔM ≈ (a_corrupt − a_clean) · (∂M ÷ ∂a evaluated on the clean run)
meaning: M is a metric such as the logit difference between the right and a wrong answer. Swapping one component's activation between a clean and a corrupted prompt shows whether that component carries the information (causal evidence, unlike probing). Attribution patching approximates every patch at once with one backward pass, a first-order Taylor estimate (∂ denotes a partial derivative).
used_for: Causal tracing in ROME (Meng and colleagues, 2022), the indirect-object-identification circuit (Wang and colleagues, 2022), attribution patching (Nanda, 2023) and AtP* (Google DeepMind, 2024). In the book: Chapter 57 (Ablation; Circuits and attribution graphs).

name: Saliency maps and gradient times input
formula: Saliency S_i = |∂F(x) ÷ ∂x_i|; gradient × input attribution_i = x_i × ∂F(x) ÷ ∂x_i
meaning: F(x) is the model's score for one output class and x_i one input feature (a pixel or a token embedding value); the partial derivative ∂F ÷ ∂x_i says how fast the score would change if that feature changed. Multiplying by the input gives a first-order estimate of each feature's contribution. Known to be noisy and sometimes misleading; SmoothGrad averages gradients over noisy copies of the input.
used_for: Simonyan and colleagues (2013) saliency maps; explanation libraries such as Captum; debugging shortcut learning in vision models. In the book: Chapter 57 (Saliency map definition, in words).

name: Integrated gradients
formula: IG_i(x) = (x_i − x'_i) × integral from α = 0 to 1 of (∂F(x' + α × (x − x')) ÷ ∂x_i) dα ≈ (x_i − x'_i) × (1 ÷ m) × sum over k from 1 to m of (∂F(x' + (k ÷ m) × (x − x')) ÷ ∂x_i); completeness: sum over i of IG_i(x) = F(x) − F(x')
meaning: Average the gradient along a straight path from a baseline input x' (a black image, an all-padding text) to the real input x, and multiply by how far each feature moved. The attributions add up exactly to the change in the model's output (completeness), a property plain gradients lack. In practice the integral is approximated with m steps, often 20 to 300.
used_for: Sundararajan, Taly and Yan (2017); Captum and cloud explainability services; attribution for vision, text and tabular models. In the book: Only here.

name: Compounding reliability over many steps
formula: P(all n steps succeed) = p^n; per-step reliability needed for a target task success T: p = T^(1 ÷ n); at least one success in k independent tries: 1 − (1 − p)^k
meaning: p is the per-step (or per-attempt) success probability and steps are assumed independent. Small per-step error rates compound fast over long tasks; the same arithmetic in reverse shows why an attacker with many attempts eventually succeeds. pass@k for capability benchmarks is owned by the classical-ML section.
used_for: Agent reliability planning; why METR's 80% time horizon is several times shorter than its 50% horizon; attack-success curves that rise with the number of attempts in jailbreak studies. In the book: Chapter 55 (From answers to actions: 0.95^20 ≈ 0.358 and the reliability table), Chapter 28, Chapter 31 (0.99^50 ≈ 61%), Chapter 57 (Try it: =1-(1-0.2)^A1).

name: Attack success rate (ASR) and refusal rates
formula: ASR = successful attacks ÷ attempts; over-refusal rate = refused benign requests ÷ benign requests; with independent attempts, ASR over k tries = 1 − (1 − ASR_1)^k
meaning: The headline numbers of red-teaming: what fraction of jailbreak or misuse attempts get through a model or a safeguard, reported together with how often harmless requests are wrongly refused (the other side of the trade-off). Results are usually given per attack method and per harm category.
used_for: Safety sections of system cards, HarmBench-style benchmarks and bug-bounty evaluations; Anthropic reported in February 2025 that automated jailbreaks succeeded 86% of the time against an unprotected model and 4.4% with constitutional classifiers. In the book: Chapter 57 (Red-teaming), Chapter 56 (Exercise: attack success rate = successes ÷ 30).

name: Expected harm (risk = probability × severity)
formula: risk = P(harm) × severity; at scale, expected incidents = rate × volume, and P(at least one incident) = 1 − (1 − p)^N
meaning: The expected loss of a risk is its probability times its size, so a rare catastrophe and a common nuisance can be compared on one scale. Multiplying a tiny per-interaction rate p by a huge number of interactions N turns rare failures into daily events.
used_for: Risk assessment in frontier safety frameworks and product safety reviews; the EU AI Act (Article 3) defines risk as the combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm. In the book: Chapter 56 (risk = probability × severity: a 1-in-1,000 chance of $1 million = $1,000), Chapter 55 (Why small error rates are big numbers: 900 million ÷ 100,000 = 9,000 a week).

name: Risk decomposition: hazard × exposure × vulnerability
formula: risk ≈ hazard × exposure × vulnerability
meaning: Hazard is the source of harm and how likely or severe it is, exposure how much of what we care about comes into contact with it, and vulnerability how easily exposed people or systems are harmed. Because the factors multiply, halving any one halves the risk, which shows where to act when a hazard cannot be removed.
used_for: Disaster-risk practice; Hendrycks and Mazeika's 'X-Risk Analysis for AI Research' (2022) and Hendrycks's 2024 textbook use it to sort safety work by the factor it reduces; AI labs cannot un-invent a capability but can cut exposure (access tiers) and vulnerability (classifiers, monitoring, patching). In the book: Chapter 56 (phishing example: 20,000 × 0.02 = 400 clicks, cut to 10,000 × 0.01 = 100).

name: Defense in depth (multiplying layer pass-through rates)
formula: pass-through = product over layers i of (1 − c_i) when layers fail independently; in general P(pass all) = P(pass layer 1) × P(pass layer 2 given passed layer 1) × ...
meaning: c_i is layer i's catch rate. Independent layers multiply small failure rates into a very small one, but layers that share blind spots fail together, and the conditional form shows how correlation destroys the benefit. This is the arithmetic of the Swiss-cheese model.
used_for: Layered safeguards around frontier models: training-time refusals, input and output classifiers (constitutional classifiers), account monitoring and access tiers, as in Anthropic's ASL-3 protections. In the book: Chapter 56 (Worked example: how layers multiply: 0.10 × 0.20 × 0.25 × 0.5 = 0.0025, versus 0.10 × 0.60 = 0.06 when classifiers share a blind spot).

name: Uplift study effect and its uncertainty
formula: uplift = mean(score with the model) − mean(score without it); SE = sqrt(s_1^2 ÷ n_1 + s_2^2 ÷ n_2); rough 95% range = uplift ± 2 × SE; relative uplift = uplift ÷ mean(control score)
meaning: s_1, s_2 are the two groups' standard deviations and n_1, n_2 their sizes. The question is not whether a model knows dangerous facts but how much it adds over ordinary tools; the standard error shows why small studies give wide ranges (four times the participants halves the range). The general two-sample statistics belong to the foundations section; this is the safety-evaluation use.
used_for: Biology and cyber uplift trials behind the capability thresholds of Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, OpenAI's Preparedness Framework and Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework; RAND's 2024 red-team study of LLM help with biological attack planning. In the book: Chapter 57 (Dangerous capability evaluations: 48 − 30 = 18 points, SE ≈ 6.3, range about 5 to 31), Chapter 56.

name: METR 50% time horizon (logistic fit) and its doubling trend
formula: P(agent succeeds on a task) = sigmoid(β × (log h_50 − log t_task)); trend: h_50(date) = h_0 × 2^((date − date_0) ÷ T_double); 80% horizon (natural logs): t_80 = h_50 × exp(−ln 4 ÷ β)
meaning: t_task is how long skilled humans take (the geometric mean of successful human attempts), β the steepness fitted per agent and h_50 the task length at which predicted success is 50%, because sigmoid(0) = 0.5. Fitting log h_50 against release dates gives a doubling time T_double. Success of 80% needs β × (ln h_50 − ln t) = ln 4, which is why the 80% horizon is several times shorter.
used_for: METR's 'Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks' (Kwa and colleagues, March 2025) found the 50% horizon doubling about every 207 days (about 7 months) since 2019, faster since 2023; METR time horizons now appear in frontier model system cards and safety evaluations. In the book: Chapter 57 (Measuring autonomy: time horizons: 4 minutes to 12 hours, about 7.5 doublings in 35 months), Chapter 24, Chapter 28, Chapter 60.

name: Private versus social expected loss (externality gap)
formula: A developer pays for extra safety work when cost < p × L_developer; society would want it when cost < p × (L_developer + L_others); externality gap = p × L_others
meaning: p is the probability of an incident, L_developer the part of the damage the developer bears and L_others the part that falls on everyone else. When most of the damage is external, the developer's calculation can say 'skip it' even when society's says 'do it', a market failure that liability rules and regulation aim to correct.
used_for: AI liability and regulation debates, insurance and safety-standard arguments. In the book: Chapter 59 (Worked example: who pays for the accident? $1 million private versus $10 million, then $100 million, social expected loss against a $50 million test).

name: Maximum expected utility (MEU)
formula: EU(a) = sum over outcomes s of (P(s given a) × U(s)); a* = argmax over a of EU(a)
meaning: U(s) is the utility (desirability) of outcome s and P(s given a) its probability if action a is taken. A rational agent picks the action with the highest probability-weighted average utility; von Neumann and Morgenstern showed that preferences obeying a few consistency rules behave as if maximizing some utility. A concave utility of money (such as ln of wealth) produces risk aversion. An MDP chains this decision over time with rewards in place of utilities.
used_for: The decision rule behind rational agents (AIMA), agents deciding whether to act or ask, and the risk calculations of the safety entries. In the book: Chapter 48 (Deciding when you are not sure: expected utility: umbrella 80 versus 70, break-even at a 20% chance of rain).

name: Value of perfect information (VPI)
formula: VPI = (sum over evidence values e of P(e) × max over a of EU(a given e)) − max over a of EU(a), which is always ≥ 0
meaning: How much better you expect to decide if you learn the evidence first: the expected utility of choosing after seeing each possible result, minus the best you can do now. Information that could not change your choice is worth zero.
used_for: Deciding when an agent should ask a clarifying question, which test to order, and active learning. In the book: Chapter 48 (radar app: 94 − 80 = 14 points).

name: Payoff matrix, dominant strategy and Nash equilibrium
formula: Nash equilibrium: u_i(s_i*, s_−i*) ≥ u_i(s_i, s_−i*) for every player i and every alternative strategy s_i; dominant strategy d: u_i(d, s_−i) ≥ u_i(s_i, s_−i) for all s_i and all s_−i
meaning: u_i is player i's payoff (one cell of the payoff matrix per combination of choices), s_i a strategy of player i and s_−i the strategies of everyone else. At an equilibrium nobody can gain by changing only their own choice; a dominant strategy is best whatever the others do. An outcome is Pareto optimal if no one can be made better off without making someone worse off, and an equilibrium need not be. Cooperative game theory's Shapley value, which splits a group's payoff fairly, is listed with SHAP in the classical-ML section.
used_for: Multi-agent RL and self-play, poker and Diplomacy AIs, AI governance analysis of racing; Nash learning from human feedback (Munos and colleagues, Google DeepMind, 2023) frames alignment as finding the equilibrium of a preference game. In the book: Chapter 48 (A short course in game theory), Chapter 59 (the racing game).

name: Prisoner's dilemma payoffs and the repeated-game cooperation threshold
formula: T > R > P > S and 2 × R > T + S; in the infinitely repeated game with discount factor δ, mutual cooperation under a grim-trigger strategy is an equilibrium when δ ≥ (T − R) ÷ (T − P)
meaning: T is the temptation payoff for defecting on a cooperator, R the reward for mutual cooperation, P the punishment for mutual defection and S the sucker's payoff. Defecting is dominant, yet both prefer mutual cooperation. If the game repeats and future payoffs matter enough (δ near 1), the threat of future punishment can sustain cooperation; tit-for-tat won Axelrod's tournaments around 1980.
used_for: Analyses of AI racing between labs and countries and of why voluntary restraint is fragile; the book's racing game has T = 9, R = 7, P = 3, S = 1, so cooperation can be sustained when δ ≥ 2 ÷ 6 ≈ 0.33. In the book: Chapter 48 (Table 48.8), Chapter 59 (Worked example: the racing game), Chapter 60 (racing dynamics).

name: Mixed-strategy equilibrium and the minimax theorem
formula: Indifference condition (two actions each): choose the opponent's mix q so that q × u(a_1, b_1) + (1 − q) × u(a_1, b_2) = q × u(a_2, b_1) + (1 − q) × u(a_2, b_2); zero-sum minimax theorem: max over x of min over y of (x^T × A × y) = min over y of max over x of (x^T × A × y)
meaning: In a mixed equilibrium each player randomizes so that the other is indifferent between their options, leaving nothing to exploit (rock-paper-scissors: one-third each). In two-player zero-sum games with payoff matrix A and mixed strategies x and y, von Neumann's theorem says the best guaranteed payoff equals the worst the opponent can hold you to: the value of the game. Minimax search over game trees belongs to the classical-AI section.
used_for: Poker bots' bluffing frequencies, security patrol scheduling, adversarial training formulations. In the book: Chapter 48 (A short course in game theory: randomness can be the best strategy; mixed strategy definition).

name: Counterfactual regret minimization (regret matching, CFR)
formula: R^T(I, a) = sum over t ≤ T of π_−i^(σ_t)(I) × (v_i(σ_t with a forced at I, I) − v_i(σ_t, I)); next strategy σ_(T+1)(I, a) = max(R^T(I, a), 0) ÷ sum over b of max(R^T(I, b), 0), or uniform if all regrets are ≤ 0
meaning: At each information set I (what a player knows at a decision point), accumulate how much better each action a would have done than the current strategy σ, weighted by the probability π_−i that the other players' and chance's moves reach I; v_i is player i's expected value. Then play actions in proportion to their positive regret. In two-player zero-sum games the average strategy converges to a Nash equilibrium. Variants: CFR+, linear and discounted CFR, Monte Carlo CFR, Deep CFR.
used_for: Zinkevich and colleagues (2007); Cepheus essentially solved heads-up limit hold'em (2015, CFR+); DeepStack and Libratus (2017) and Pluribus (2019, six-player no-limit hold'em) beat top professionals. In the book: Chapter 48 (Poker: Libratus and Pluribus; CFR definition).

name: Expected-value model of an AI race
formula: EV_i = sum over possible winners j of P(j wins) × [(1 − d(s_j)) × U_i(j wins safely) + d(s_j) × U_disaster], where d(s) is the chance of disaster given the winner's safety effort s (for example d = 1 − s) and less safety effort raises a team's chance of winning
meaning: Each team trades safety for speed: skimping raises P(win) but also the chance d that the winner's system causes a disaster. U_i(j wins safely) is lower for rivals than for oneself, by an amount Armstrong, Bostrom and Shulman (2016, 'Racing to the precipice') call enmity. In their model more competing teams and more enmity push equilibrium safety down, and teams learning each other's capabilities can make it worse; check the paper's exact parameterization before quoting numbers.
used_for: AI governance arguments for coordination, verification and compute-based agreements. In the book: Chapter 59 (Worked example: the racing game), Chapter 60 (racing dynamics).

name: Second-price (Vickrey) auction and truthful bidding
formula: Winner = highest bidder, who pays the second-highest bid b_(2); bidder utility u_i = v_i − b_(2) if i wins, else 0; bidding b_i = v_i is a dominant strategy
meaning: v_i is what the item is worth to bidder i. Because your bid only decides whether you win, not what you pay, overbidding risks paying more than the value and underbidding risks losing a profitable win, so honesty is optimal: mechanism design making truth-telling the best strategy. Its multi-slot cousin, generalized second-price pricing for ads, is not truthful in general and is listed with ad ranking in the classical-ML section.
used_for: Mechanism design in AIMA; the incentive logic behind sponsored-search and ad-exchange auctions (many exchanges moved to first-price auctions by 2019); spectrum auctions. In the book: Chapter 48 (You can design the game: sealed-bid second-price auction), Chapter 51.
